passages.t: Two kinds of counsel at Shechem
passages.happening:
Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king (verse 1). Jeroboam returns from Egypt, and the people say, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you should lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you” (verse 4).

The elders who served Solomon answer, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever” (verse 7). Rehoboam rejects their counsel and asks the young men who grew up with him. They tell him to say that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist (verse 10), and ‘Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke’ (verse 11). He answers the people harshly (verses 12-14). ‘So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God, in order that the LORD might fulfill the word that He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Solomon's splendor had cost heavy labor and taxes, and now the bill comes due. This is the great turning point of 2 Chronicles: the kingdom of David and Solomon breaks apart, around 931 BC. From here on the book follows the kings of Judah, though it never stops calling the north Israel or hoping for its return.

The Chronicler follows 1 Kings 12 almost word for word, but he leaves out 1 Kings 11: Solomon's idolatry, the adversaries God raised, and Ahijah's tearing of his cloak into twelve pieces to give Jeroboam ten. Verse 15 refers to that prophecy as something his readers already know. Jeroboam, an Ephraimite whom Solomon had put over the labor of the house of Joseph, had fled to Egypt and found refuge with Shishak. Shechem was an old center of the northern tribes, where Joshua had renewed the covenant; Rehoboam had to go there to be accepted, and the north's loyalty was not automatic.

Kingship in Israel was a covenant. David had been made king over the north by a covenant with its elders, and the assembly expected terms: the people would serve the king if he lightened their load. The elders' counsel, etsah, reflects the ideal of the king as a shepherd who wins loyalty by serving. The yoke, ol, comes seven times. Rehoboam's reply is crude and boastful; some think waist carries a vulgar double meaning, and the scorpions may be barbed whips or simply a picture of pain.
passages.later: A proverb says, ‘A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger’ (Proverbs 15:1). Ahijah had told Jeroboam, ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes’ (1 Kings 11:31).
passages.hard:
If the division was from God, was Rehoboam to blame?

Verse 15 says the turn of events was from God, to fulfill his word through Ahijah. The word for turn of events, nesibbah, is found only here. Readers ask whether this makes God the author of Rehoboam's folly or frees Rehoboam from blame.

The Bible holds both that God governs history and that people answer for their choices. Rehoboam freely rejected wise counsel out of pride, the text presents it as his decision, and the consequences fall on him. At the same time God had already said the kingdom would be divided because of Solomon's idolatry, and he worked through Rehoboam's pride to bring it about. Christian theologians explain this in different ways. Some stress that God ordains all events while never being the author of sin; others stress his foreknowledge and his use of human choices he permits rather than causes. The same pattern appears in the story of Joseph and in the crucifixion as Acts tells it. The text does not resolve the philosophical question, but it will not let either truth cancel the other.
passages.asks: The elders told Rehoboam that if he served the people they would serve him forever. Ask whom you lead, at home, at work or in a church, and whether you lighten their load or add to it. And ask whose counsel you seek when you have already decided what you want to hear.

passages.happening: When all Israel sees that the king will not listen, they answer, “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!” (verse 16). Rehoboam reigns only over the Israelites living in Judah's cities (verse 17). He sends Hadoram, who is over the forced labor, and the Israelites stone him to death; Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem in his chariot (verse 18). ‘So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The cry To your tents echoes the rebel Sheba's cry against David in 2 Samuel 20: a call to go home and withdraw allegiance. The question about their portion, cheleq, in David is a formal renunciation. The northern tribes declare that they have no share in David's house.

Sending the man in charge of forced labor to negotiate was the worst possible choice; he was the face of the grievance itself. The closing line, to this day, is taken over from Kings. By the Chronicler's own time the northern kingdom had long since fallen to Assyria, and yet he still calls its people Israel.
passages.later: Second Samuel tells of Sheba son of Bichri, who shouted, “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” (2 Samuel 20:1).
passages.asks: The people asked for a lighter load and were met with contempt, and a kingdom broke. Ask whether there is someone whose request you have answered with pride. And ask what it would cost you to go back and answer kindly.
